title: Level 1: Show a Message
summary: Use the print block to make the program say something.

steps.instruction: Welcome to Beginner mode. We build real programs one block at a time. A program is a stack of blocks the computer runs top to bottom. Press Continue when you are ready.
steps.screenReaderHint: Beginner mode, Level 1. We will make the program print a message. Press the Continue button to begin.

steps.instruction: From the Text category in the toolbox, add a print block to the workspace. A print block shows a message when the program runs.
steps.screenReaderHint: Open the toolbox, choose the Text category, and place the print block. With the keyboard: press T to open the toolbox, move to Text, then place the print block onto the workspace.
steps.successText: Print block added. It already holds a small text slot that says abc.

steps.instruction: The print block came with a text value that says "abc". Change that text to your own message, for example your name or "Hello".
steps.screenReaderHint: Edit the text inside the print block. Move the cursor onto the text value and type a new message to replace abc.

steps.instruction: Now run the program. Press the Run button. Your message appears in the Output panel.
steps.screenReaderHint: Activate the Run button to run your program. The output panel will read your message.
steps.successText: It ran. Your message printed to the output.

steps.instruction: That is a whole program: a print block with a message, run to produce output. Press Continue to finish Level 1.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 1 recap. You added a print block, set its message, and ran it. Press Continue to complete the level.

hints: The print block lives in the Text category of the toolbox.
Place the print block on an empty part of the workspace first.
To change the message, edit the text value that sits inside the print block.
The Run button is above the workspace; the result shows in the Output panel.

title: Level 2: Numbers and Math
summary: Do a calculation with number and arithmetic blocks, and print the result.

steps.instruction: Computers are great at math. The Math category has number blocks and an arithmetic block that adds, subtracts, multiplies, or divides. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 2. We will build a calculation and print its answer. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Math category, add an arithmetic block. It comes with two number slots and a plus sign between them.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the arithmetic block from the Math category. It has two number inputs joined by an operator you can change.

steps.instruction: Change at least one of the two numbers in the arithmetic block to a value other than 1.
steps.screenReaderHint: Edit one of the number values inside the arithmetic block. Replace the default 1 with another number.

steps.instruction: Add a print block and drop the arithmetic block into the print block's message slot, so the program prints the answer.
steps.screenReaderHint: Connect the arithmetic block into the print block's text input, replacing its text value, so the calculation result is what gets printed.
steps.successText: The calculation is now wired into the print block.

steps.instruction: Run the program. The answer to your calculation appears in the Output panel.
steps.screenReaderHint: Activate Run. The output reads the numeric result of your arithmetic.
steps.successText: Level 2 complete. You printed a calculated answer.

hints: The arithmetic block is in the Math category; it has two number slots.
Click or move onto a number value to type a different number.
The operator in the middle can be changed to plus, minus, times, or divide.
Drop the arithmetic block into the print block where its text value used to be.

title: Level 3: Remember a Value
summary: Store a value in a variable and use it again.

steps.instruction: A variable is a labelled box that remembers a value so you can use it later. The Variables category lets you make one. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 3. We will create a variable, store a value in it, and print it. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: In the Variables category, create a variable, then add a "set" block that stores a value into it.
steps.screenReaderHint: Open the Variables category, create a new variable, and place a set block. The set block assigns a value to your variable.
steps.successText: Set block added — your variable can now hold a value.

steps.instruction: Add a print block, then place a "get" version of your variable into the print so the program shows what the variable holds.
steps.screenReaderHint: Add a print block and drop a variable get block into its text slot, so printing reads the variable's stored value.
steps.successText: The print now reads your variable.

steps.instruction: Run the program. It prints whatever value you stored in the variable.
steps.screenReaderHint: Activate Run. The output reads the value your variable holds.
steps.successText: Level 3 complete. Variables let you reuse a value by name.

hints: Use the Variables category to create a variable first; give it a clear name.
The set block reads: set [name] to [value].
Put a number or text block into the set block's value slot.
The get block is the rounded variable block you drop into the print.

title: Level 4: Build Text
summary: Join pieces of text together and inspect text.

steps.instruction: You can glue text together to build sentences. The "create text with" block joins several pieces into one. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 4. We will join text pieces and print the combined result. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Text category, add the "create text with" block. It has slots for two pieces of text.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the create-text-with block from the Text category. It joins multiple text values into one string.

steps.instruction: Put a text value into the join block and type a word into it, such as "Hello ".
steps.screenReaderHint: Add a text value into one of the join block's slots and type a word into it.

steps.instruction: Drop the join block into a print block, then run the program to see the joined text.
steps.screenReaderHint: Connect the join block into a print block's text slot, then run to print the combined text.
steps.successText: Level 4 complete. You combined pieces of text into one message.

hints: The create-text-with block is in the Text category.
Each slot of the join block takes its own text value.
Type directly into a text value to change what it says.
Drop the whole join block into the print block's message slot.

title: Level 5: True and False
summary: Compare values and work with true/false results.

steps.instruction: Programs make decisions using true and false. A compare block checks two values and answers true or false. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 5. We will compare two numbers and print whether the result is true or false. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Logic category, add a compare block. It checks two values with a sign like equals, less than, or greater than.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the compare block from the Logic category. It compares a left value and a right value.

steps.instruction: Put a number into each side of the compare block. Use two different numbers.
steps.screenReaderHint: Add a number value to the left and right inputs of the compare block, using two different numbers.
steps.successText: The comparison has values to check.

steps.instruction: Drop the compare block into a print block and run it. The output says true or false.
steps.screenReaderHint: Connect the compare block into a print block's slot, then run. The output reads true or false.
steps.successText: Level 5 complete. Comparisons give you true or false to decide with.

hints: The compare block is in the Logic category.
Change the middle sign to equals, less than, or greater than.
Each side of the compare takes a number value.
Print the compare block to see its true or false result.

title: Level 6: Make a Decision
summary: Use an if block to run code only when a condition is true.

steps.instruction: An if block runs the blocks inside it only when its condition is true. Add an else part and it runs something different when the condition is false. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 6. We will build an if block that prints one thing when true and another when false. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Logic category, add an if block to the workspace.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the if block from the Logic category. It has a condition slot and a body that runs when the condition is true.

steps.instruction: Put a condition into the if block: drop a compare block or a true/false block into its condition slot.
steps.screenReaderHint: Add a condition to the if block by connecting a compare block or a boolean true/false block into its IF slot.
steps.successText: The if block has a condition to test.

steps.instruction: Inside the if block's body, add a print block so something happens when the condition is true. Then run it.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a print block inside the if block's do-section, then run the program.
steps.successText: Level 6 complete. Your program now decides what to do.

hints: The if block is in the Logic category.
The condition slot sits at the top of the if block.
Reuse a compare block from Level 5 as the condition.
Put the print block inside the if block's body, not below it.

title: Level 7: Repeat Something
summary: Use a repeat loop to run blocks several times.

steps.instruction: A loop repeats blocks for you instead of copying them. The repeat block runs its body a set number of times. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 7. We will repeat a print several times with a loop. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Loops category, add the "repeat" block. It already has a number telling it how many times to repeat.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the repeat block from the Loops category. It repeats its body a set number of times.

steps.instruction: Put a print block inside the repeat block's body so the message repeats.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a print block inside the repeat block's do-section.
steps.successText: The print is now inside the loop.

steps.instruction: Run the program. Your message prints once for each repeat. Try changing the repeat count and running again.
steps.screenReaderHint: Activate Run. The output repeats your message for the number of times set on the loop.
steps.successText: Level 7 complete. Loops save you from repeating yourself.

hints: The repeat block is in the Loops category.
The number on the repeat block sets how many times it runs.
Put the print block inside the loop's body so it repeats.
Change the count to a small number like 3 to keep the output short.

title: Level 8: Loop Until Done
summary: Use a while loop that repeats while a condition stays true.

steps.instruction: A while loop keeps repeating as long as its condition is true. Useful when you don't know the exact number of repeats ahead of time. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 8. We will build a while loop with a condition. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Loops category, add the "repeat while" block.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the repeat-while block from the Loops category. It repeats while its condition is true.

steps.instruction: Give the while loop a condition: drop a true/false block or a compare block into its condition slot.
steps.screenReaderHint: Connect a boolean or compare block into the while loop's condition slot.
steps.successText: The while loop has a condition.

steps.instruction: Put a print block inside the while loop's body. Caution: a condition that is always true repeats forever, so plan to keep it short. Press Continue when your loop has a body.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a print block inside the while loop's body, then press Continue.
steps.successText: Level 8 complete. While loops repeat until their condition turns false.

hints: The repeat-while block is in the Loops category.
Its condition slot is at the top, like the if block.
A boolean true/false block is the simplest condition to start with.
Keep the body small; an always-true condition never stops on its own.

title: Level 9: Lists of Things
summary: Make a list and read items out of it.

steps.instruction: A list holds many values in order, like a shopping list. You can read items, count them, and loop over them. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 9. We will make a list and print something about it. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Lists category, add the "create list with" block. Fill at least two of its slots with text values.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place the create-list-with block from the Lists category and add text values to its slots.

steps.instruction: Add a "length of" block and drop your list into it, so you can count how many items the list has.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a length-of block and connect your list into it to count its items.
steps.successText: You can now measure the list's length.

steps.instruction: Drop the "length of" block into a print block and run it. The output shows how many items are in your list.
steps.screenReaderHint: Connect the length-of block into a print block, then run. The output reads the item count.
steps.successText: Level 9 complete. Lists let you handle many values together.

hints: The create-list-with block is in the Lists category.
Each slot of the list takes its own value; text values work well.
The length-of block counts the items in a list.
Print the length-of block to see the count when you run.

title: Level 10: Make Your Own Block
summary: Define a function once and call it to reuse it.

steps.instruction: A function is a block you define yourself: name a set of steps once, then run them any time by calling that name. This is how big programs stay tidy. Press Continue.
steps.screenReaderHint: Level 10, the capstone. We will define a function and call it. Press Continue.

steps.instruction: From the Procedures category, add a "to do something" function-definition block, and give your function a name.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a function-definition block from the Procedures category and name your function.

steps.instruction: Put a print block inside your function definition, so the function does something when called.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a print block inside the function definition block's body.
steps.successText: Your function now has a body.

steps.instruction: Now add a call block for your function on the main workspace and run the program. Calling the function runs its steps.
steps.screenReaderHint: Place a call block for your function in the main program and run. The output shows the function's print.
steps.successText: Level 10 complete. You defined a function and called it — that completes Beginner mode!

hints: The function-definition block is in the Procedures category.
Name your function something clear, like greet.
Whatever you put inside the definition runs when the function is called.
After defining it, the Procedures category shows a call block for your function.
